article.title: California Election Results 2026: Statewide Races, Propositions and Los Angeles Returns
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. California’s election returns present a mixed picture for the candidates and ballot positions listed in the LA Progressive November 2026 Voter Guide . Xavier Becerra holds a substantial statewide lead for governor, Jane Kim leads for insurance commissioner, and many congressional and legislative candidates in the guide are ahead. But several are trailing, and statewide voters are taking a different course from Los Angeles County on some major propositions. The distinction matters most for Proposition 4, concerning public campaign financing, and Proposition 40, the billionaire wealth tax. Both have more Yes than No votes in Los Angeles County. Both are trailing statewide. This report combines the Secretary of State’s statewide and full-district returns with Los Angeles County returns for local races. Every lead described below refers to ballots counted so far. Even where the state lists all precincts as reporting, that does not establish that every eligible ballot has been counted or that results are certified. Statewide offices: Becerra leads, with Kim ahead in the insurance race Xavier Becerra has 4,992,161 votes, or 63.9%, against Steve Hilton’s 2,815,459 votes, or 36.1%, in the governor’s contest. Becerra is the candidate listed in our guide. The guide-listed candidates also lead for lieutenant governor, secretary of state, controller, treasurer, attorney general and superintendent of public instruction. The insurance commissioner contest is closer: Jane Kim leads Ben Allen, 52.0% to 48.0%, a margin of 265,576 votes. In Board of Equalization District 3, Sam Sukaton trails Mike Gipson: 707,476 votes, or 40.5%, to Gipson’s 1,038,750 votes, or 59.5%. These are the Secretary of State’s full-district figures. State propositions: public financing and wealth tax trail Proposition 4 has 3,599,779 Yes votes, or 48.0%, and 3,892,816 No votes, or 52.0%. The No side leads by 293,037 votes. LA Progressive’s guide listed Yes. Proposition 40 has 3,419,652 Yes votes, or 44.4%, against 4,280,110 No votes, or 55.6%. Its No side leads by 860,458 votes. The guide also listed Yes on this measure. Proposition 42 offers another contrast with Los Angeles County: its Yes side leads statewide with 54.3%, while the guide listed No. Proposition 38’s Yes side leads with 55.7%, also running against the guide’s No position. Other returns align with the guide. Proposition 39’s No side leads with 58.6%; Proposition 44’s No side has 81.8%. Proposition 5 is much closer, with Yes ahead by 48,425 votes, 50.3% to 49.7%. The following table uses statewide totals throughout. “Aligned” means the side currently ahead matches the guide’s listed position; it is not a declaration of passage or defeat. Congress: full-district totals change the picture in District 23 Tessa Lynn Hodge leads within Los Angeles County’s portion of Congressional District 23, but trails across the full district. The Secretary of State reports 63,681 votes for Hodge, or 48.7%, and 67,169 for Jay Obernolte, or 51.3%. Obernolte’s advantage is 3,488 votes. Angela Gonzales-Torres leads Jimmy Gomez in District 34, 58.7% to 41.3%, while Angélica María Dueñas trails Luz Maria Rivas in District 29, 39.8% to 60.2%. Salud Carbajal, Raul Ruiz and Pete Aguilar—whose contests were absent from the supplied county results—each lead in their full districts. All congressional figures below cover the entire district, including every county portion reported by the Secretary of State. State Legislature: Duncan holds a narrow lead Chris Duncan leads Tony Strickland in Senate District 36 by just 1,060 votes: 141,285 to 140,225, or 50.2% to 49.8%. His much larger percentage advantage within Los Angeles County does not reflect how close the full-district contest is. John Erickson trails Brian Goldsmith in Senate District 24, while Sarah Rascón trails Sara Hernandez in District 26. In Assembly District 51, Colin Hernandez—the candidate listed in the guide’s October 31 update—has 37.2%, behind Rick Chavez Zbur’s 62.8%. The full-district count also supplies results for several Assembly contests missing from the county page. James Ramos, Leila Namvar, Clarissa Cervantes and Corey Jackson lead; Victor Hernandez and Kevin Akin trail. State Senate State Assembly Two guide entries need clarification. Assembly District 50 lists DeJonaé Shaw in the guide, but the Secretary of State’s returns list Robert Garcia and Victoria Viveros Mageno. Assembly District 54 lists John Yi in the guide, while the returns list Mark Gonzalez and Alexandra Briseno. Neither Shaw nor Yi can be assigned a general election result from these returns. The tables retain the guide entries and mark the mismatch explicitly. The Senate District 20 table uses the ballot spelling Caroline Menjivar; the guide spells her first name “Carolyn.” Juan Carrillo’s surname is also standardized to the ballot spelling. Los Angeles: Raman leads Bass, Roy leads for city attorney In the county’s 3:11 a.m. update, Nithya Raman leads Karen Bass by 16,594 votes: 377,458 to 360,864, or 51.12% to 48.88%. Bass is the candidate listed in the guide. Marissa Roy, also listed in the guide, leads John McKinney for city attorney, 66.13% to 33.87%. Both City Council candidates in the guide trail: Barri Worth Girvan is 823 votes behind Timothy Gaspar in District 3, and Estuardo Mazariegos is 1,936 behind Jose Ugarte in District 9. For county sheriff, Robert Luna leads Alex Villanueva, 68.53% to 31.47%. Judicial and community college races remain mixed Justin Allen Clayton leads in Superior Court Office 65. Rhonda Haymon trails Maria Ghobadi in Office 64, and David Ross trails Donna Tryfman in Office 131. The guide lists both candidates in Office 87: A.J. Bayne leads David DeJute, 54.42% to 45.58%, so that contest cannot fairly be treated as a single guide candidate’s success or setback. For the Los Angeles Community College District board, Steve Veres leads the Seat 2 field and Darryn Harris leads Seat 4. Gabriel Buelna is second to Randall Winston in Seat 6. Local measures: mixed alignment with the guide County Measure E’s Yes side leads with 72.86%, aligning with the guide’s Yes position. County Measure A’s Yes side leads with 64.53%, despite the guide’s No position. All eight Los Angeles city measures listed in the guide currently have more Yes than No votes. That aligns with the guide on LA, PL, PRK, PRT and FD, and runs against its No positions on EE, SC and TE. The work continues as ballots are counted These returns show why an election assessment must look beyond party labels or a single county’s vote. Candidates listed in the guide hold many leads, but some of the policies it favored face substantial statewide opposition. Close contests such as Senate District 36 and Proposition 5 deserve particular attention as counting proceeds. For LA Progressive readers, the immediate task is to follow the count accurately. The larger task remains holding those who take office accountable for housing, public services, civil rights, democratic participation and the distribution of political power. An election determines who holds office; organizing helps determine what they do with it. Sources and timing: Statewide offices, state propositions and complete congressional and legislative districts use the California Secretary of State’s November 4, 2026, 8:08 a.m. update. Local offices and measures use Los Angeles County’s November 4, 2026, 3:11:55 a.m. update. These snapshots have different reporting times. No race is called in this article.
